name: Euler Critical Buckling Load
description: Gives the Euler critical load at which a slender column buckles, π²EI/(KL)². The effective length factor K accounts for the end supports, so the load falls sharply as the column gets longer.
notes: Valid only for long, elastic, initially straight columns below the material yield stress. Use consistent SI units (Pa, m^4, m) for a result in newtons.

name: Simply Supported Beam End Slope (Uniform Load)
description: Gives the rotation at each support of a simply supported beam under a uniform load, wL³/(24EI). This end slope grows with the cube of the span and shrinks with beam stiffness EI.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a uniformly distributed load along the whole span. Result is in radians; keep w, L, E and I in consistent SI units.

name: Euler Buckling Stress
description: Gives the critical Euler buckling stress of a column, π²E/λ², where λ is the slenderness ratio. More slender columns (higher λ) buckle at much lower stress, independent of cross-sectional area.
notes: Valid only in the elastic range; the result must stay below the material yield stress or buckling theory does not apply. The slenderness ratio λ is dimensionless.

name: Cantilever Beam Max Deflection (End Point Load)
description: Gives the maximum deflection at the free end of a cantilever with a point load there, PL³/(3EI). Deflection grows with the cube of the length and drops as the flexural stiffness EI rises.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a load applied at the free tip. Use consistent SI units for a result in meters; a stiffer or shorter beam deflects far less.

name: Cantilever Beam Deflection (Uniform Load)
description: Gives the free-end deflection of a cantilever under a uniform distributed load, wL⁴/(8EI). The fourth-power dependence on length makes long cantilevers deflect dramatically under distributed loading.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a load spread evenly over the full length. Keep w, L, E and I in consistent SI units for a result in meters.

name: Simply Supported Beam Center Deflection (Point Load)
description: Gives the midspan deflection of a simply supported beam with a central point load, PL³/(48EI). It is the maximum deflection for this symmetric case and scales with the cube of the span.
notes: Assumes the load is exactly at midspan and small elastic deflections. Use consistent SI units for a result in meters; off-center loads need a different formula.

name: Simply Supported Beam Max Deflection (Uniform Load)
description: Gives the midspan maximum deflection of a simply supported beam under a uniform load, 5wL⁴/(384EI). The deflection rises with the fourth power of the span and falls with flexural stiffness EI.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a load uniformly distributed over the whole span. Keep units consistent in SI for a result in meters.

name: Fixed-Fixed Beam Center Deflection (Point Load)
description: Gives the midspan deflection of a beam fixed at both ends with a central point load, PL³/(192EI). The built-in ends make it four times stiffer than the simply supported case, so deflection is much smaller.
notes: Assumes fully rigid (clamped) supports at both ends and small elastic deflections. Use consistent SI units for a result in meters.

name: Cantilever Beam End Slope (Point Load)
description: Gives the rotation at the free end of a cantilever carrying a tip point load, PL²/(2EI). This end slope grows with the square of the length and decreases with flexural stiffness EI.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a load at the free tip. Result is in radians; keep P, L, E and I in consistent SI units.

name: Simply Supported Beam Support Slope (Point Load)
description: Gives the rotation at each support of a simply supported beam with a central point load, PL²/(16EI). This slope quantifies how much the beam ends tilt under the symmetric load.
notes: Assumes the point load is at midspan and small elastic deflections. Result is in radians with consistent SI units for P, L, E and I.

name: Cantilever Deflection from End Moment
description: Gives the free-end deflection of a cantilever loaded by a moment at its tip, ML²/(2EI). A pure end moment bends the beam into a circular arc, and the tip deflection scales with the square of the length.
notes: Assumes small elastic deflections and a constant moment producing uniform curvature. Use consistent SI units for a result in meters.

name: Elastic Beam Curvature (M/EI)
description: Gives the curvature of an elastic beam under a bending moment, M/(EI), the reciprocal of the radius the beam bends into. Curvature is proportional to the moment and inversely proportional to the flexural stiffness EI.
notes: Valid for small elastic deflections within the linear (Euler-Bernoulli) range. Result has units of 1/m; keep M, E and I in consistent SI units.

name: Radius of Curvature of Bent Beam
description: Gives the radius of curvature of a beam bent by a moment M, EI/M, the radius of the circular arc the neutral axis follows. A larger moment or a less stiff beam produces a tighter (smaller-radius) bend.
notes: Valid for small elastic deflections in the linear range; it is the reciprocal of the beam curvature. Use consistent SI units for a result in meters.

name: Max Transverse Shear Stress (Rectangular Beam)
description: Gives the peak transverse shear stress in a solid rectangular beam cross-section, which occurs at the neutral axis. It equals 1.5 times the average shear stress (shear force V divided by area A), reflecting the parabolic shear distribution.
notes: Valid only for solid rectangular sections; other shapes use different factors (4/3 for circular). Peak is at the neutral axis, not the extreme fibers where bending stress is largest.

name: Max Transverse Shear Stress (Circular Beam)
description: Gives the peak transverse shear stress in a solid circular beam cross-section, occurring at the neutral axis. It equals 4/3 of the average shear stress, the ratio of shear force V to cross-section area A.
notes: Applies to solid circular sections only; rectangular sections use a factor of 1.5. The maximum acts at the neutral axis, distinct from the location of maximum bending stress.

name: Transverse Shear Stress (VQ/It)
description: Computes the transverse shear stress at a point in a beam cross-section using the shear formula. It multiplies the shear force V by the first moment of area Q above the point, divided by the moment of inertia I and the section width t at that level.
notes: Q is the first moment of the area outside the plane where stress is evaluated, and t is the width there; both change with position, so the stress varies across the depth.

name: Thermal Stress in Constrained Bar
description: Gives the stress that develops in a bar fully restrained against thermal expansion when its temperature changes by dT. It equals Young's modulus times the thermal expansion coefficient times the temperature change, since the prevented strain becomes elastic stress.
notes: Assumes complete restraint with no length change; partial restraint gives lower stress. A temperature rise produces compression, a drop produces tension. Result is independent of the bar's length or area.

name: Rule of Mixtures — Voigt (Longitudinal Modulus)
description: Estimates the longitudinal elastic modulus of a fiber composite loaded along the fibers, using the Voigt (equal-strain) rule of mixtures. It is the volume-weighted average of the fiber and matrix moduli based on the fiber volume fraction Vf.
notes: Vf is a fraction between 0 and 1 (not a percent), and the matrix fraction is 1-Vf. Valid for loading parallel to continuous aligned fibers; it gives an upper bound on stiffness.

name: Rule of Mixtures — Reuss (Transverse Modulus)
description: Estimates the transverse elastic modulus of a fiber composite loaded across the fibers, using the Reuss (equal-stress) rule of mixtures. It is the inverse of the volume-weighted average of the compliances of fiber and matrix.
notes: Vf is a fraction from 0 to 1, and 1-Vf is the matrix fraction. This equal-stress model applies to loading perpendicular to the fibers and gives a lower bound on stiffness.

name: Radius of Gyration of Section
description: Computes the radius of gyration of a cross-section, defined as the square root of the moment of inertia I divided by the area A. It represents the distance from the axis at which the whole area could be concentrated to give the same inertia.
notes: I and A must refer to the same axis. Used in column buckling as the slenderness ratio L/r; a smaller radius of gyration means a more slender, buckling-prone member.

name: Hydrostatic Pressure at Depth
description: Gives the gauge pressure exerted by a static fluid at depth h below its surface. It equals the fluid density times gravitational acceleration times the depth, increasing linearly with how deep the point lies.
notes: This is gauge pressure above the surface value; add atmospheric pressure for absolute pressure. Assumes constant density and a fluid at rest. Depth is measured vertically from the free surface.

name: Hydrostatic Force on Submerged Plane
description: Computes the total hydrostatic force on a submerged flat plate. It equals the fluid density times gravity times the depth of the plate's centroid hc times the plate area A, i.e. the pressure at the centroid acting over the area.
notes: hc is the vertical depth of the centroid, not the top edge. The force uses centroid pressure, but its line of action (center of pressure) lies deeper than the centroid.

name: Depth of Center of Pressure
description: Gives the vertical depth to the center of pressure on a submerged plane surface, where the resultant hydrostatic force acts. It equals the centroid depth hc plus the centroidal second moment Ic divided by the product of hc and area A.
notes: Ic is the second moment of area about the centroidal axis. The center of pressure always lies below the centroid; the offset shrinks as the surface is submerged deeper.

name: Simple Beam Reaction (Asymmetric Point Load)
description: Computes the support reaction at one end of a simply supported beam carrying a single point load P placed off-center. It equals P times b divided by the span L, where b is the load's distance from the opposite support.
notes: b is measured from the far support, so this returns the reaction at the near support. The closer the load sits to a support, the larger that support's reaction. Ignores beam self-weight.

name: Axial Strain Energy in Bar
description: Computes the elastic strain energy stored in an axially loaded bar. It equals the load P squared times the length L, divided by twice the product of cross-section area A and Young's modulus, representing the work stored in stretching the bar.
notes: Assumes linear-elastic material, uniform axial stress, and a constant cross-section carrying a constant load P along its length. Doubling the load quadruples the stored energy.

name: Bending Strain Energy in Beam
description: Computes the elastic strain energy stored in a beam under a constant bending moment. It equals the moment M squared times the length L, divided by twice the product of Young's modulus and the moment of inertia I.
notes: Valid for a uniform beam with a constant moment M along its length; for varying moment, the energy must be integrated. Assumes linear-elastic bending. Energy scales with the square of the moment.

name: Torsional Stiffness of Shaft
description: Gives the torsional stiffness of a circular shaft, the torque required per unit angle of twist. It equals the shear modulus G times the polar moment of inertia J divided by the shaft length L.
notes: Valid for a uniform circular shaft in the linear-elastic range. For non-circular sections J must be replaced by a torsion constant. A longer shaft is more compliant (lower stiffness).

name: Angle of Twist of Shaft
description: Computes the angle of twist of a circular shaft under an applied torque. It equals the torque T times the length L, divided by the product of the shear modulus G and the polar moment of inertia J, and is returned in radians.
notes: Result is in radians; multiply by 180/pi for degrees. Assumes a uniform circular shaft with constant torque in the linear-elastic range. Non-circular sections require a torsion constant instead of J.

name: Polar Moment of Inertia (Hollow Circular Shaft)
description: Computes the polar moment of inertia of a hollow circular shaft, a measure of its resistance to torsion. It equals pi times the difference of the outer and inner diameters raised to the fourth power, divided by 32.
notes: D and d are diameters, not radii; the fourth-power difference must use diameters consistently. Requires D greater than d. For a solid shaft set d to zero.

name: Section Modulus (Hollow Circular Section)
description: Computes the elastic section modulus of a hollow circular section in bending. It equals pi times the fourth-power difference of outer and inner diameters, divided by 32 times the outer diameter D, giving the moment of inertia over the outer radius.
notes: D and d are diameters. Bending stress equals moment divided by this section modulus, so a larger value means lower stress. Requires D greater than d.

name: Plastic Section Modulus (Rectangular Section)
description: Computes the plastic section modulus of a solid rectangular section, used to find its fully plastic bending capacity. It equals the width b times the height h squared, divided by 4.
notes: This is the plastic modulus Z, larger than the elastic modulus (bh^2/6); their ratio is the shape factor 1.5 for rectangles. h is the depth in the bending direction. Plastic moment equals Z times yield stress.

name: Allowable Stress from Safety Factor
description: Computes the allowable design stress by dividing the material's yield strength sy by a chosen factor of safety FS. The result is the maximum stress the design permits while keeping a margin below yielding.
notes: FS is a dimensionless value greater than 1. Based on yield strength here; using ultimate strength instead gives a different allowable. A larger factor of safety yields a more conservative (lower) allowable stress.

name: Factor of Safety (Yield)
description: Computes the factor of safety against yielding as the ratio of the material's yield strength sy to the actual working stress sigma. It indicates how many times the applied stress could increase before reaching yield.
notes: Dimensionless; a value below 1 means the working stress already exceeds yield. Based on yield strength, not ultimate. Both stresses must be expressed in the same units.

name: Maximum Principal Stress (Plane Stress)
description: Computes the maximum principal (normal) stress at a point in plane stress. It is the average of the two normal stresses plus the radius of Mohr's circle, formed from half their difference and the shear stress txy.
notes: Applies to a two-dimensional plane-stress state. Tension is positive; sign conventions matter. This gives the maximum principal stress; the minimum uses a minus sign before the square root.

name: Maximum In-Plane Shear Stress
description: Computes the maximum in-plane shear stress at a point in plane stress, equal to the radius of Mohr's circle. It is the square root of the square of half the normal-stress difference plus the shear stress txy squared.
notes: This is the in-plane maximum; the absolute maximum shear may be larger once the out-of-plane principal stress is considered. Uses a two-dimensional plane-stress state with consistent sign conventions.

name: Thin-Walled Spherical Pressure Vessel Stress
description: Computes the membrane (wall) stress in a thin-walled spherical pressure vessel under internal pressure. It equals the pressure p times the radius r divided by twice the wall thickness t, and is equal in all directions.
notes: Valid only for thin walls (radius at least about ten times thickness). Uses internal gauge pressure. A sphere's wall stress is half that of a cylinder's hoop stress at the same p, r, t.

name: Cantilever Beam Fundamental Frequency
description: Estimates the fundamental natural frequency of a uniform cantilever beam. It scales with the square root of bending stiffness Ey·I over mass per length mu and the fourth power of length L, using the first-mode eigenvalue constant.
notes: The 3.5156/tau factor converts the first-mode eigenvalue to a frequency in hertz. Assumes a uniform slender beam fixed at one end and free at the other. Frequency drops sharply as length increases.

name: Shear Flow in Built-Up Beam
description: Computes the shear flow, the shear force per unit length, that must be transferred between parts of a built-up beam at a joint. It equals the shear force V times the first moment of area Q divided by the moment of inertia I.
notes: Q is taken for the area connected by the joint about the neutral axis. Shear flow sizes the fasteners or welds: divide by fastener spacing to get the force each must carry.

name: Fixed-End Moment (Central Point Load)
description: Gives the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support of a fixed-fixed beam carrying a central point load P. It equals the load P times the span L divided by 8.
notes: Applies to a beam fixed at both ends with the load at midspan; the end moments and the midspan moment are all PL/8 in magnitude. Load must be central; off-center loads use different formulas.

name: Fixed-End Moment (Uniform Load)
description: Gives the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support of a fixed-fixed beam carrying a uniformly distributed load w. It equals the load intensity w times the span L squared divided by 12.
notes: For a beam fixed at both ends under a full-span uniform load. w is load per unit length. The midspan moment is smaller (wL^2/24) and of opposite sign to these end moments.

name: Elastic Strain Energy Density
description: Computes the elastic strain energy stored per unit volume in a uniaxially stressed material. It equals the stress sigma squared divided by twice Young's modulus, i.e. the area under the linear stress-strain curve per unit volume.
notes: Valid in the linear-elastic range under uniaxial stress; beyond yield this underestimates the true energy. When sigma equals the yield stress this gives the modulus of resilience.

name: Hertzian Maximum Contact Pressure (Spheres)
description: Estimates the maximum contact pressure between two elastic spheres pressed together, from Hertzian contact theory. It is the cube root of six times the force F and effective modulus Estar squared, over pi cubed times the effective radius Reff squared.
notes: Estar and Reff are the combined (effective) modulus and radius of the two bodies. Assumes frictionless, non-conforming elastic contact with small deformations well below yield.

name: Beam on Elastic Foundation Characteristic Factor
description: Computes the characteristic factor (often called beta) for a beam resting on an elastic foundation. It is the fourth root of the foundation modulus kf divided by four times the beam bending stiffness Ey·I, and sets the decay length of deflections.
notes: Its reciprocal, 1/beta, is the characteristic length over which loads spread. kf is the foundation stiffness per unit length. A stiffer foundation gives a larger beta and more localized response.

name: Torsional Shear Stress (Hollow Shaft)
description: Computes the maximum torsional shear stress at the outer surface of a hollow circular shaft. It equals the torque T times the outer diameter D divided by twice the polar moment of inertia Jp (equivalently T·r/Jp with r the outer radius).
notes: Uses the outer diameter, so it gives the peak stress at the outer fiber; stress falls linearly to a minimum at the inner surface. Jp must be the polar moment for the hollow section.

name: Coordinate Area of a Triangle (Shoelace)
description: Computes the area of a triangle from the plane coordinates of its three vertices using the shoelace (cross-product) formula. The absolute value makes the result independent of the order in which vertices are listed.
notes: All coordinates share a length unit (m), giving area in square meters. The formula is exact for any triangle regardless of shape; without the abs, vertex order would give a signed area.

name: Slope Angle from Percent Grade
description: Converts a percent grade (rise over run times 100) into the corresponding slope angle in degrees by taking the arctangent of the grade fraction. A 100 percent grade equals a 45 degree slope.
notes: Grade is entered as a percent value, not a fraction; the formula divides by 100. The relationship is nonlinear, so grade and angle are not proportional except at small slopes.

name: Horizontal Distance from Slope Distance
description: Reduces a measured slope distance L to its horizontal projection by multiplying by the cosine of the vertical angle. This is the plan distance used for mapping and area computation.
notes: L is in meters and the angle in degrees; the result is in meters. The vertical angle is measured from the horizontal; a zero angle returns the full slope distance unchanged.

name: Vertical Distance from Slope Distance
description: Computes the vertical component (elevation difference) of a measured slope distance L by multiplying by the sine of the vertical angle. It gives the rise or fall between the two ends of the line.
notes: L is in meters and the angle in degrees; the result is in meters. The vertical angle is measured from the horizontal; a positive angle gives a rise, a negative one a fall.

name: Stadia Distance (Inclined Sight)
description: Computes the horizontal distance in stadia tacheometry for an inclined sight, from the stadia interval s, the multiplying constant K, the additive constant C, and the vertical angle. It reduces the staff intercept to plan distance.
notes: s and C are in meters, the angle in degrees; K is dimensionless (usually 100). The cosine is squared here for the horizontal reduction; for an exactly level sight it becomes the simple K*s + C.

name: Stadia Elevation Difference
description: Computes the elevation difference in stadia tacheometry for an inclined sight, from the stadia interval s, constants K and C, and the vertical angle, using the half-sine-of-double-angle term. It gives the rise or fall to the staff point.
notes: s and C are in meters, the angle in degrees; K is dimensionless. This gives only the instrument-to-staff-point height component; instrument height and staff reading must still be applied for a true reduced level.

name: Combined Curvature and Refraction Correction
description: Estimates the combined correction in meters for Earth curvature and atmospheric refraction over a sight distance D in kilometers, using the standard 0.0675 D squared rule for leveling and trigonometric heighting.
notes: D is in kilometers and the result is in meters. The 0.0675 constant already nets curvature (which lowers the sight) against refraction (which raises it), assuming a standard refraction coefficient of about 0.13.

name: Earth Curvature Correction (Leveling)
description: Estimates the correction in meters due to Earth curvature alone over a sight distance D in kilometers, using the 0.0785 D squared rule. Curvature makes a level line drop away from the horizontal with distance.
notes: D is in kilometers and the result is in meters. This is the curvature effect only, without refraction; the combined curvature-and-refraction correction uses a smaller constant because refraction partly offsets it.

name: Allowable Angular Misclosure
description: Gives the permissible angular misclosure of a traverse as the instrument least count k times the square root of the number of angles n, reflecting how random angular errors accumulate over a closed traverse.
notes: k is in arcseconds and n is a count; the result is in arcseconds. The square-root growth assumes independent random errors; a measured misclosure larger than this indicates a blunder to investigate.

name: Sum of Interior Angles (Polygon Traverse)
description: Gives the theoretical sum of the interior angles of a closed polygon traverse with n sides, equal to (n minus 2) times 180 degrees. It is the check total against which measured angles are balanced.
notes: n is the number of sides (and interior angles); the result is in degrees. Valid for simple (non-self-intersecting) polygons; the measured angle sum should be adjusted to equal this value.

name: Relative Precision of a Traverse
description: Expresses a traverse's relative precision as the perimeter divided by the linear misclosure, giving the denominator of a ratio such as 1 in 20000. A larger value means a more precise, better-closing traverse.
notes: Perimeter and misclosure share the unit (m), so the result is dimensionless and read as 1 in that number. Compare against the survey's required precision standard to accept or reject the traverse.

name: Volume by Average End Area
description: Estimates the earthwork volume between two cross-sections by averaging their end areas A1 and A2 and multiplying by the length L between them. It is the standard average-end-area method for cut and fill.
notes: L is in meters and areas in square meters, giving volume in cubic meters. It slightly overestimates for concave shapes; the prismoidal formula is more accurate when a mid-section area is available.

name: Prismoidal Volume Formula
description: Computes the volume of an earthwork prismoid from its two end areas A1 and A2, the mid-section area Am, and the length L, weighting the middle area four times. It is more accurate than the average-end-area method.
notes: L is in meters and areas in square meters, giving cubic meters. The mid-section area Am must be measured at the true midpoint, not averaged from the ends, or the accuracy advantage is lost.

name: Contour Spacing on a Grade
description: Computes the horizontal spacing between successive contour lines for a given contour interval and ground grade, equal to the contour interval divided by the grade fraction. Steeper ground packs contours closer together.
notes: Contour interval is in meters and grade is a percent value; the result is in meters. The grade is divided by 100 internally; the spacing assumes a uniform grade between the contours.

name: Area by Trapezoidal Rule (Offsets)
description: Computes the area between a survey baseline and an irregular boundary using the trapezoidal rule over equally spaced offsets, giving the end offsets half weight and the interior offset full weight, times the offset interval d.
notes: d and the offsets are in meters, giving square meters. This example uses three offsets; the rule assumes the boundary is straight between offsets and needs equal spacing d.

name: Simpson's One-Third Rule (Area)
description: Computes the area between a baseline and a curved boundary using Simpson's one-third rule over equally spaced offsets, weighting the middle offset four times and the ends once, times one-third of the interval d.
notes: d and the offsets are in meters, giving square meters. It fits parabolic arcs between offsets and so needs an even number of intervals (odd number of offsets) with equal spacing; it is more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for curved boundaries.

name: Height of Instrument (Leveling)
description: Computes the height of instrument (line of sight elevation) in differential leveling by adding the backsight reading BS to the known elevation of the benchmark BM. It establishes the collimation level for computing other points.
notes: Benchmark elevation and backsight are in meters; the result is in meters. The backsight is always added because it is a reading taken on a point of known elevation; foresights are later subtracted.

name: Reduced Level from Foresight
description: Computes the reduced level (elevation) of a point in differential leveling by subtracting the foresight reading FS from the height of instrument HI. This yields the ground elevation at the staff position.
notes: Height of instrument and foresight are in meters; the result is in meters. The foresight is subtracted because a larger staff reading means the ground is lower relative to the line of sight.

name: Tape Temperature Correction
description: Computes the length correction for a steel tape used at a field temperature differing from its standardization temperature, as the expansion coefficient times the temperature difference times the measured length. It corrects for thermal expansion.
notes: The coefficient is per degree Celsius, temperatures in Celsius, and length in meters; the result is in meters. The correction is positive (add) when the field temperature exceeds the standard temperature.

name: Tape Pull Correction
description: Computes the elongation of a tape when the applied pull differs from the standard pull, as the pull difference times the length divided by the product of the cross-sectional area and Young's modulus. It corrects for elastic stretch.
notes: Pull in newtons, length in meters, area in square meters, and modulus in pascals give a result in meters. The correction is positive when applied pull exceeds standard pull; it assumes elastic behavior of the tape.

name: Tape Sag Correction
description: Computes the correction for the sag of a tape suspended between supports, which always makes the measured distance longer than the true chord. It equals the weight per length squared times the span cubed over 24 times the pull squared.
notes: Weight per length in N/m, span in meters, and pull in newtons give a result in meters. The sag correction is always subtracted from the measured length; higher tension sharply reduces it via the pull-squared term.

name: Slope Correction (Taping)
description: Approximates the correction to subtract from a slope-measured length to get horizontal distance, using half the elevation difference squared divided by the slope length. It is the small-angle approximation of the slope reduction.
notes: Elevation difference h and slope length L are in meters; the result is in meters and is always subtracted. Valid only for gentle slopes where h is small relative to L; use the exact cosine reduction for steep lines.

name: Sea-Level Reduction Correction
description: Computes the correction to reduce a distance measured at mean elevation H down to its equivalent length at sea level, as the length times elevation over Earth's radius. It accounts for the shrinking of the arc toward the geoid.
notes: Length, elevation, and Earth radius must share a unit (meters); the result is in meters and is subtracted. The correction grows with elevation; at sea level it is zero.

name: Subtense Bar Distance
description: Computes the horizontal distance to a subtense bar of known length b from the small angle it subtends at the instrument, as half the bar length divided by the tangent of half the subtended angle. It gives distance without taping.
notes: Bar length b is in meters and the angle in degrees; the result is in meters. The bar must be set horizontal and perpendicular to the line; accuracy falls off rapidly as distance grows and the subtended angle shrinks.

name: Degree of Curve from Radius (Arc)
description: Converts a horizontal curve radius R into its degree of curve (arc definition) in degrees, the central angle subtended by a 100-unit arc, equal to 5729.578 divided by R. A smaller radius gives a sharper, higher-degree curve.
notes: The constant 5729.578 (equal to 100 times 180 over pi) assumes a 100-unit arc, so R must be in the same length unit as that station length; this is the arc definition, distinct from the chord definition.

name: Clothoid Parameter (Spiral Curve)
description: Computes the clothoid parameter A, which defines the geometry of a spiral (transition) curve connecting a straight and a circular curve of radius R over a spiral length Ls.
notes: A is often used to look up standard spiral tables. A larger A gives a gentler, more gradual transition; A equals the radius at the point where the spiral's radius of curvature equals its own length.

name: Spiral Angle (Clothoid)
description: Computes the spiral angle θs, in degrees, swept by a clothoid transition curve of length Ls joining a circular curve of radius R.
notes: θs is the angle between the initial tangent and the tangent at the spiral-to-curve (SC) point. Keep Ls and R in the same length unit.

name: Minimum Spiral Length (Shortt's Formula)

variables.label: Rate of change of radial acceleration

description: Estimates the minimum length of a spiral transition curve using Shortt's formula, from the design speed V, curve radius R, and an allowable rate of change of radial (centripetal) acceleration C.
notes: C is typically taken between 0.3 and 0.6 m/s³ for passenger comfort; a smaller C gives a longer, more comfortable transition.

name: Curve Length (Circular Arc)
description: Computes the arc length L of a circular curve from its radius R and central (deflection) angle Δ.
notes: Δ is the total angle between the back and forward tangents, entered in degrees.

name: Tangent Length (Circular Curve)
description: Computes the tangent length T, the distance from the point of curvature to the point of intersection (PI) of a circular curve, from radius R and central angle Δ.
notes: T = R·tan(Δ/2); Δ is entered in degrees.

name: External Distance (Circular Curve)
description: Computes the external distance E, the offset from the point of intersection (PI) to the midpoint of a circular curve, from radius R and central angle Δ.
notes: E = R·(sec(Δ/2) − 1); Δ is entered in degrees.

name: Middle Ordinate (Circular Curve)
description: Computes the middle ordinate M, the distance from the midpoint of the long chord to the midpoint of a circular curve, from radius R and central angle Δ.
notes: M = R·(1 − cos(Δ/2)); Δ is entered in degrees.

name: Long Chord Length (Circular Curve)
description: Computes the long chord length C connecting the start and end points of a circular curve, from radius R and central angle Δ.
notes: C = 2R·sin(Δ/2); Δ is entered in degrees.

name: K-Value (Vertical Curve Rate)
description: Computes the K-value of a parabolic vertical curve, the horizontal distance needed for a 1 percent change in grade, from curve length L and the algebraic difference in grades A.
notes: A larger K-value means a flatter, more gradual vertical curve; K is commonly checked against minimum sight-distance requirements.

name: Vertical Curve Offset (Parabolic)
description: Computes the vertical offset y between the tangent line and the parabolic curve at distance x from the beginning of a vertical curve (BVC), given the grade difference A and curve length L.
notes: y is measured perpendicular to the horizontal, not along the tangent grade line. At x = L, y equals the full tangent offset.

name: Minimum Curve Radius (Superelevation & Side Friction)
description: Computes the minimum horizontal curve radius R that keeps a vehicle at design speed V safely on the curve, given the superelevation rate e and side friction factor f.
notes: e and f are entered as decimals, e.g. 0.06 for 6 percent superelevation. The constant 127 applies when V is in km/h and R is in meters.

name: Minimum Clothoid Parameter (Design Speed)

variables.label: Rate of change of radial acceleration

description: Computes the minimum clothoid parameter A required for a comfortable spiral transition at design speed V, using an allowable rate of change of radial acceleration C. Because A² = R·Ls and Shortt's formula makes Ls proportional to 1/R, the radius R cancels out: the minimum A depends only on speed and comfort, not on the chosen curve radius.
notes: This is the same relationship as Shortt's formula (minimum spiral length), rearranged so that R drops out. It is a quick way to check the minimum clothoid parameter for a given design speed before a specific radius has been chosen.

name: Rankine Active Earth Pressure Coefficient
description: Computes the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient Ka=tan²(45°-φ/2) for a cohesionless soil with internal friction angle φ. Ka relates the lateral active pressure a retaining wall must resist to the vertical overburden pressure.
notes: Friction angle φ is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians. Assumes a smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill, and no cohesion, per the classic Rankine assumptions.

name: Terzaghi Ultimate Bearing Capacity (Strip Footing, General Shear)
description: Computes the ultimate bearing capacity of a strip footing by Terzaghi's general shear equation, qu=c·Nc+q·Nq+0.5·γ·B·Nγ, combining cohesion, surcharge, and soil weight contributions.
notes: The bearing capacity factors Nc, Nq and Nγ depend only on the soil friction angle φ and must be looked up from a Terzaghi table or chart for the given φ before entering them here. Assumes a strip footing under general shear failure on a homogeneous soil.

name: Reinforced Concrete Beam Moment Capacity (Whitney Stress Block)
description: Computes the nominal moment capacity Mn of a singly reinforced concrete beam using the Whitney rectangular stress block, Mn=As·fy·(d-a/2) with equivalent stress block depth a=As·fy/(0.85·f'c·b) substituted inline.
notes: Use consistent SI units (m² for As, Pa for fy and f'c, m for d and b) to get Mn in newton-metres. Assumes a singly reinforced, tension-controlled section per ACI-style Whitney block assumptions; does not check reinforcement ratio limits.

name: Traverse Latitude (Coordinate Geometry)
description: Computes the latitude (north-south coordinate component) of a traverse course of length L and bearing angle θ, as L×cos(θ). It is used with the departure to compute coordinate differences between traverse stations.
notes: The bearing angle θ is entered in degrees, measured from the reference (usually north) meridian, and converted internally to radians. The sign convention for the bearing must be applied consistently when summing a full traverse.

name: Traverse Departure (Coordinate Geometry)
description: Computes the departure (east-west coordinate component) of a traverse course of length L and bearing angle θ, as L×sin(θ). It is used with the latitude to compute coordinate differences between traverse stations.
notes: The bearing angle θ is entered in degrees, measured from the reference (usually north) meridian, and converted internally to radians. The sign convention for the bearing must be applied consistently when summing a full traverse.

name: Building Coverage Ratio (建蔽率)
description: Computes the building coverage ratio (建蔽率), the percentage of a site's area covered by a building's footprint, as footprint area divided by site area times 100. It is a key zoning limit on ground-floor building extent.
notes: Both areas must share the same unit (square metres). Local zoning codes set a maximum allowable percentage that the building footprint may not exceed.

name: Floor Area Ratio (容積率)
description: Computes the floor area ratio (容積率), the percentage relationship between a building's total floor area across all stories and its site area, as total floor area divided by site area times 100. It caps the overall building bulk permitted on a site.
notes: Total floor area sums the floor area of every story, including basements per local code definitions. Both areas must share the same unit (square metres); zoning codes set a maximum allowable percentage.

name: Water-Cement Ratio
description: Computes the water-cement ratio used in concrete mix design, the mass of mixing water divided by the mass of cement times 100. It is the single most important factor controlling concrete strength and durability.
notes: Both masses must share the same unit (kilograms). A lower ratio generally gives higher strength and durability but reduces workability; typical structural mixes fall roughly between 40 and 60 percent.

name: Earthwork Volume Conversion by Soil Factor
description: Converts an earthwork volume measured in one soil state to another by a soil conversion factor, V2=V1×factor. Using the loosening coefficient L (typically around 1.1-1.3) converts bank volume to loose (excavated) volume, while using the compaction coefficient C (typically around 0.85-0.95) converts bank volume to compacted volume.
notes: Enter the appropriate coefficient for the conversion needed: an L-value greater than 1 for loose/hauled volume, or a C-value less than 1 for compacted/finished volume. Coefficients are soil-specific and should come from geotechnical data or local earthwork standards.

name: Simplified Allowable Bearing Capacity from SPT N-value
description: Estimates the allowable bearing capacity of sandy soil from its Standard Penetration Test blow count N, using the simplified empirical relation qa≈30+0.6·N. It gives a quick preliminary check before a full geotechnical analysis.
notes: Intended as a rough, conservative first estimate for cohesionless (sandy) soils only; it is not a substitute for a full bearing capacity analysis. N is the raw or corrected SPT blow count depending on the convention used locally.

name: N-value to Internal Friction Angle (Dunham's Formula)
description: Estimates the internal friction angle φ of sandy soil from its Standard Penetration Test blow count N using Dunham's formula, φ=sqrt(15·N)+15. It provides a quick empirical friction angle for use in bearing capacity or earth pressure calculations.
notes: Applicable to sandy (cohesionless) soils; several variants of Dunham's formula exist for different grain shapes and gradations, so treat the result as an approximation. N should be the SPT blow count appropriate to the convention used locally.
